Limpopo Parks

By: Johann Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Limpopo's provincial parks are struggling. Is it a lack of money, or could it be corruption?

Summary:
Blouberg Nature Reserve in Limpopo province is struggling to make ends meet like most provincial reserves. The proposed budget shows an expenditure of R7000 per month for this reserve for the next year. This is less than 10% of the minimum needed to manage the reserve. An organisation called The Friends of Blouberg have been helping to keep the reserve going for the past few years. However, the reserve is also under land claims, which hasn't been settled yet. For the past three years the limpopo government have allowed the land claimants to do hunting of 10 - 15 buffalo on this reserve annually to make some money. This is problematic because it is not a hunting reserve and you now have a situation where hunters and tourists are driving around the same park. When questioned about this, Limpopo government said the hunting allowance was part of the co-management agrement between the provincial government and the land claimants. However, a copy of this agreement obtained by the Friends of Blouberg shows that there is no mention of hunting at all. To make matters worse the hunting comes down to a huge financial loss for the province the reserve and the people of South Africa who ultimately own the buffalo.

Further information:
These buffalo are so-called "clean" buffalo meaning that they are clean of bovine TB and thus worth a lot more money than non-clean buffalo. A clean buffalo today sells for between R300 000 and R900 000 each. At an average of R500 000 per buffalo it means that the annual worth of the buffalo is at least R5million rand. The land claimants only pay R1000 per permit, meaning the province only get R10 000 for the R5 000000 worth of buffalos. The claimants then put the buffalo out on tender and according to this years figures only got R20 000 per buffalo, The rest of the money is then made by the hunting outfitter who sources overseas hunters. of Blouberg have suggested an alternative for the hunting which entails removing 10 buffalo per year and putting them into a recognised breeding programme and selling the offspring, splitting the money earned between the land claimants and the reserve to cover the running costs. They are prepared to do this with no money coming to themselves. Yet the government and the claimants are refusing to even consider this offer

Extra Budget Items:
Three trips to Limpopo, covering 5000km's and 8 different reserves.
8 filming days with cameraman

Mr. Barry Fourie
Mr. Chris Vorster Professional Hunting Outfitter

Blouberg Nature Reserve

Press Release:


Limpopo Province boasts 43 provincial reserves. But how well are they managed? Our investigation shows that we stand a real chance of losing most of them is something doesn't change soon.

Script:


Studio intro
Politically and socially, Limpopo is a complex province. It was made up of the old Northern Transvaal and bits and pieces of 5 of the 10 so called homelands from the apartheid era. This means that the post 94 government has to represent people from many different ethnic, race and social groups. With an 80% unemployment rate and with more than two thirds of all dwellings in the province being on tribal or communal land, this is the poorest of our 9 provinces. Its two biggest potential sources of income are mining and tourism.


Buffalo walking. V/o before shot
It's late afternoon, and what this lone Kruger buffalo probably doesn’t know, is that he’s crossed the open border between Kruger and Letaba Ranch, one of the adjoining Limpopo Provincial reserves. Something draws his attention and he comes to investigate.
What he also probably doesn’t know, is that in this park, hunting is allowed.
Shots fired
Link John
Hunting in itself is an emotional issue. But when the animals being hunted are from the Kruger park, that emotion is taken to an entirely new level.

But although the hunting of Kruger animals may upset many South Africans, it is all done legally, and the 43 provincial reserves in Limpopo, face many more serious problems, that could threaten their existence. The department that manages them is LEDET, Limpopo Economic Development, Environment and Tourism. Judging by their budget, it is clear that conservation and potential tourism in these parks is not a strategic priority for government. Ledet says that their budget for conservation is R120.5million. But 93% is allocated to staff costs, leaving only 7% for operations. Divided by the 43 reserves, this works out to just under R200 000 per reserve per annum. Compare that to for example, the catering budget of R1080 000.00 per year. On top of it, the reserves don't even get the R200 000 – it sits in a centralised budget at head office, and they have to ask for every cent they need – and often this either takes months, or they just get told that there aren’t any funds left.
Although their official tourism website says day visitors are welcome here and even though head office assured us we would be welcome to film in the parks, we couldn’t get past the gate.
Upsound
Let me just phone the reserve manager, he just stepped out for a moment.

But Chris Vorster ,who has been hunting in Letaba Ranch for more than 20 years, says he can see the decay...
Chris Vorster
As of lately, you can see for yourself, things are not going well in Letaba Ranch. The management of Ledet is not up too scratch at the moment. The people on the ground....but if they don't get the funds and they don't get the tools from headoffice, they cant do their job.

But it's not all about lack of funding. Bad planning, or simply a lack of caring also seems to play a major role. Chris says the animals in the southern part of the park have always been dependent on manmade watering holes. Last summer, LEDET decided to upgrade these working boreholes to solar powered units. Work started and all the pipes were pulled out, and then suddenly they abandoned the project, leaving the animals stranded with no water.
Chris Vorster
You can see the heat. And we're going to have this heat wave and its going longer and longer.No. Animals are dying physically inside here.

But Ledet says they are maintaining the boreholes, and no dead animals have been reported...
By law, each reserve has to have a management plan. The first 28 reserves were done in 2011/2012, and although the MEC has signed them off, most management plans have only been partially implemented – due to a claimed lack of funding. But according to our source, they have no intention of implementing them.

Just outside Lephalale is D'Nyala reserve, and according to the same website, they are open and boast fantastic facilities.
John Link
In its heyday D'Nyala was one of the crown jewels in the Limpopo Province. It was so popular that it would often play host to the previous administration's “Bosberaad” meetings. Today, it's avery different story.
V/o
For starters, the reserve is not open to the public as the website indicates. The infrastructure inside the park has collapsed. Ledet says that National department of Environment, DEA has approved R29million rand to fix this. But even the guard seems to have his doubts about this.
Upsound: Guard:
Hulle kom nie deur nie. Ek wag. Ek sit met my hande so en dan ek luister en ek kyk. Partykeer hulle kom hierso: “Nee, ons soek daai ding. Hulle meet van daar af tot hierso. Maar o “Nee, jy sal sien. Oor twee dag of drie dag dan kom ek” Maar (he whistles)
V/o
Just under 50% of posts are vacant and more than 50% of the rangers that are employed, are over 50 years of age. This means that they can't really patrol or do the hard field work anymore and SANBI has had to step in with another 109 younger people to help on the ground. This means an average of 2.5 extra people per reserve, clearly not enough to solve the problem. Also, the 43 reserves have between them, only 26 appointed reserve managers.

They also have a desperate shortage of scientists. There are no ecologists left in the department, and the support team for the entire province comprises of one zoologist, one aquatic specialist and a herpetologist. Scientific work either has to be outsourced at great cost or is just not done.

Officially, Bewaarkloof is still a reserve. But the local community was successful in their land claim and, according to Ledet, the community did not want to enter into an official agreement with the department. On the road we took, there was no gate and no fence, and not a single ranger in sight. The park is totally overrun by people, who have openly set up homes and built kraals for their cattle kilometers inside the reserve. We saw numerous men hunting with their dogs, but perhaps the most shocking was seeing how commercial woodgathering had become a free for all. All big trees within reach have been chopped down and now they are aiming for the younger ones. They told us that they could get R300/load by donkey car and R650 for a truck load. The incessant clanging of cattle bells drives home the irony of the name “Bewaarkloof” or Conservation Valley..
Link:John
Masebe Reserve in the Waterberg is situated in one of the most scenic parts of the country if not the entire continent. It is precisely the type of place a foreign tourist would love to see as part of that once-in-a-lifetime expedition.
V/o:
Once again the website says they are open, but archive footage from 2010 already showed severe decay. The facilities were built at a cost to the taxpayer of just under R6-million. The guard says they've been closed for more than two years. Ledet blames lack of funds for the collapse and say they now need R49million to fix and upgrade the reserve.
The only income the community stakeholders are getting, is a grazing levy paid by the state, and an annual hunting quota, to control the game numbers. But even though they deny it, we’ve heard from various sources that game counts throughout the province is haphazard affair, and often done at the wrong time of the year - so the numbers are at best, a thumb suck.

Not far from masebe, is Blouberg…
John
Blouberg is of critical importance, because it is home to one of the largest breeding colonies of cape vulture to be found on the african continent.

To try and save Blouberg from the same fate as the other reserves, a number of private environmentalists started the Friends of Blouberg.
Barry
Ons het n groter vlughok gebou vir die jong aasvoels. Die hok het omtrent 'n R100 000 gekos, wat ons by borge gekry het.
Die vorige trekker het nie meer agterwiele gehad nie, ons het vir hom twee splinternuwe wiele opgesit.
Bo by die uitkykpunt waar die jong aasvoels vrygelaat word het ons n dubbeldoel.. mense kan daar gaan sit en oor die berg uitkyk en goeters. By voorbeel voor slaan hy oop. Dan kan die aasvoels bietjie van 'n launching pad he wanneer hulle vrygelaat word.

But while they struggle to raise a few pennies for Blouberg, Ledet has been awarding hunting quotas to the land claimants.

Blouberg's buffalos are so called clean or disease-free animals, making them worth between R200 000 and R400 000 each. Yet the community only pays the permit fee and then sells these animals to a hunting outfitter for around R60 000 per animal.
Barry
Hoe kan hulle staatsbates verkoop?

Friends of Blouberg suggested that they would rather take the animals, at their own expense, and put them in a breeding programme. The valuable offspring can then be sold and the money split between the reserve, the community and LEDET. This would earn millions for the cash strapped department, but LEDET says that they already have buffalos in a breeding programme, and that this option does not fit into their game reduction plan.

At first Ledet told Barry that hunting was part of the co-management agreement with the land claimants, but when he finally got hold of the document, there was no mention of hunting in it. They now say that they act on endorsement by the department of Rural Development and land reform and that it is acceptable to issue the quotas to land claimants, even before these communities have become the rightful land owners.

According to their strategic management plan the Rural Land Claims Commission ruled that the co-management agreement was illegal, but Ledet denies any knowledge of this, and in 2015 they issued another hunting quota to the community
Barry
Hulle het ses geskiet – dis R360 000

Ledet refused to appear on camera, but sent us a written response to some of our questions,

But the fact is that they don't really own these parks or the animals – they are merely the custodians who do it on our behalf, and with our money. Therefore they should be accountable. We stand a real chance of losing most of these 43 provincial reserves, including all the biodiversity that already needs protection – not to mention animals like these three bulls from Kruger, who also ended up on the wrong side of the invisible fence.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Limpopo's provincial parks are struggling. Is it a lack of money, or could it be corruption?
metadata.Summary: Blouberg Nature Reserve in Limpopo province is struggling to make ends meet like most provincial reserves. The proposed budget shows an expenditure of R7000 per month for this reserve for the next year. This is less than 10% of the minimum needed to manage the reserve. An organisation called The Friends of Blouberg have been helping to keep the reserve going for the past few years. However, the reserve is also under land claims, which hasn't been settled yet. For the past three years the limpopo government have allowed the land claimants to do hunting of 10 - 15 buffalo on this reserve annually to make some money. This is problematic because it is not a hunting reserve and you now have a situation where hunters and tourists are driving around the same park. When questioned about this, Limpopo government said the hunting allowance was part of the co-management agrement between the provincial government and the land claimants. However, a copy of this agreement obtained by the Friends of Blouberg shows that there is no mention of hunting at all. To make matters worse the hunting comes down to a huge financial loss for the province the reserve and the people of South Africa who ultimately own the buffalo.
metadata.Further information: These buffalo are so-called "clean" buffalo meaning that they are clean of bovine TB and thus worth a lot more money than non-clean buffalo. A clean buffalo today sells for between R300 000 and R900 000 each. At an average of R500 000 per buffalo it means that the annual worth of the buffalo is at least R5million rand. The land claimants only pay R1000 per permit, meaning the province only get R10 000 for the R5 000000 worth of buffalos. The claimants then put the buffalo out on tender and according to this years figures only got R20 000 per buffalo, The rest of the money is then made by the hunting outfitter who sources overseas hunters. of Blouberg have suggested an alternative for the hunting which entails removing 10 buffalo per year and putting them into a recognised breeding programme and selling the offspring, splitting the money earned between the land claimants and the reserve to cover the running costs. They are prepared to do this with no money coming to themselves. Yet the government and the claimants are refusing to even consider this offer
